newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Labour saps Conservative support from business.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Labour saps Conservative support from business.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major suffered another election campaign blow on Monday with two new polls showing his support ebbing among Britain's business community.

With its well-being closely tied to the success of the economy, business has traditionally shunned the opposition Labour Party, fearful of its reputation as the tax and spend ally of trade unions and the low paid.
But two polls released on Monday showed a majority of business leaders are unconcerned about the prospect of a Labour government after the May 1 election.

"The government now faces a double whammy. Their policies are failing to fire the imagination and managers are no longer having nightmares at the prospect of a Labour government," said Roger Young, director general of the Institute of Management (IM) which conducted one of the polls.
The survey found Major's support among managers hit a new low of 40 percent in March, having fallen from 62 percent at the general election in 1992.
But Labour leader Tony Blair's strenuous efforts to shed his party's high tax image and present a more business-friendly face have not entirely convinced managers.

While leading opinion polls give Labour around 55 percent of support in the country -- a commanding 25-point lead -- the party's support among business at 25 percent remained well below the Conservatives, although still nearly double its 13 percent level in 1992.
Major has emphasised the country's economic success and business-friendly environment in his quest for re-election, strongly warning of the risks of a left-wing Labour government.
But another poll found the ruling Conservatives were not being rewarded for improvements in the economy since the recession of the early 1990s.

In a survey of 748 companies by Reed Personnel Services, a recruitment specialist, 78 percent of British businesses reported that a government change would either make no difference to their success or improve it, while 18 percent said they would be less successful under Labour.
Conservatives could take some solace as only 15 percent reported they would be more successful under a new regime.
More senior managers felt a change of government would make their organisations more successful than middle managers or support staff, the poll reported.

The IM survey found that 45 percent of managers did not believe a Labour government would adversely affect the UK's competitiveness and 47 percent did not believe the party would give too much power to trade unions.

Despite the decline in support for Conservatives, the poll showed broad consensus on tax and public spending. Eighty percent said it was time for a fundamental review of the services the state should supply and the levels of tax needed to support those services.
